title: What Tokyo Said When Nagasaki Stopped Responding
fullText: Tokyo is trying to reach Nagasaki. Nobody answers. It is 11:30 in the morning on August 9th, 1945. [music] In a military communications room somewhere in the capital, an operator sits at his station, headphones [music] pressed to his ears, transmitting into silence. The frequency is clear. The equipment is working. There is simply no one on the other end. 28 minutes earlier, something happened to Nagasaki. No one in Tokyo knows what yet. 3 days before this, Tokyo tried to reach Hiroshima. That silence, they told themselves, [music] was a one-time event. The Americans had built one weapon, used it, [music] and spent it. The war could still be won. Now, the operator adjusts his frequency, and tries again. Still nothing. In the six days that follow this moment, three [music] separate catastrophes will converge on Tokyo with enough force to break a government. What will actually make surrender possible is something else entirely. And it will cost one man everything he had. Japan in August 1945 is not a nation deciding whether to fight. [music] It is a nation that has been fighting for 14 years and does not know how to stop. By the time summer arrives, the math is beyond dispute. American submarines and aerial mining campaigns have strangled the supply lines. The Imperial Navy no longer has enough fuel reserves to put its ships to sea. The Great Fleet reduced to floating anti-aircraft platforms anchored in harbors going nowhere. The 1945 rice harvest has collapsed, the worst in 35 years. Tokyo burned in March. One night, [music] 100,000 dead. Most of the country's major cities are ash and foundation. Their population scattered and [music] underfed. The arithmetic of starvation is already running. And yet the government has a plan. It is called operation ketu go. And it depends on a single assumption. The Americans will eventually have to [music] land. The logic has its own internal coherence. make the invasion so costly, so saturated with casualties that Washington negotiates rather than absorb another 100,000 dead. Kamicazi [music] aircraft by the thousands. Citizens drilled to charge tanks with bamboo spears. Every beach minded, every hill fortified, every [music] last grain of soil turned into a killing ground. Not a strategy for victory. A strategy for survival on terms that preserve the Imperial House. Desperate, [music] yes, but not without its own reasoning. Not to the men who built it. Six men control whether this strategy lives or dies. They are the supreme council for the direction of the war. Known later as the big six. The prime minister, the foreign minister, [music] the army minister, the navy minister, the army chief of staff, and the navy chief of staff. Under Japan's governing structure, they can act only in anonymity. [music] Any single member can veto peace. The architecture of the system was [music] designed to project strength. In August 1945, it is a trap. Three of them want to fight. Three of them want to stop. General Korachica Anami is 57 years old, broadshouldered with the bearing of a man who has spent his life in [music] command. As army minister, he is Ketu Go's loudest advocate and its human embodiment. [music] He wears the uniform of the Imperial Japanese Army the way other men wear their names. He has never questioned whether Japan should fight, only how and with what ferocity. He is about to be placed inside a situation that those questions [music] cannot answer. Across the table from him, in every meeting that matters, sits foreign minister Shiggonori Togo, a career diplomat, trim and precise, with wire- rimmed glasses [music] and a reputation for bluntness unusual in these rooms. He was brought back into government because the peace [music] faction needed someone who understood what the Potdam Declaration actually offered. He understands it. He has read it with a lawyer's precision, and he is not afraid to say in a room full of generals exactly what the numbers say. By August 9th, these six men have not reached agreement. One word from any one of them ends the possibility of peace. Before either side can move, the peace faction is operating on an assumption that is already dead. For months, Japan has been sending diplomatic overtures to Moscow. The logic seems sound. The Soviet Union holds a non-aggression pact with Japan that does not expire until 1946, and Soviet self-interest appears to favor keeping Japan as a buffer state rather than allowing an American occupation of the Pacific. If anyone can broker a negotiated peace, one with conditions rather than unconditional surrender, surely it [music] is Moscow. What Tokyo does not know cannot know is that Stalin made his commitment to the Allied cause at Thran and at Yaltta. While Japanese diplomats have been waiting for a Soviet reply, [music] nearly 1 and a half million Soviet troops have been quietly redeploying from the European theater to the Manurion border. Roads surveyed, supply chains finalized, timetable set. Every week Tokyo spends waiting for Moscow is a week the Soviet military spends advancing the clock. The trap has been set for months. Japan is walking into it blind. Then there is the question of Hiroshima. On August 6th at 8:15 in the morning, the Anola Gay drops an atomic bomb on a city of 340,000 people. Confused reports reach Tokyo that afternoon and then remarkably almost nothing happens. The army and navy offer something close to a collective [music] shrug. The argument at the highest levels of government is that Hiroshima was a singular event. The Americans had built one weapon, used it, and the board was unchanged. The Supreme Council does not convene a formal meeting. 3 days pass. [music] There is, however, one private exception. On the afternoon of August the 8th, the emperor summons Togo to his residence. What he says in that meeting will become one of the most consequential private conversations of the war. He tells the foreign minister the situation is becoming impossible. The war must end. He has made his decision. His government has not. In the early hours of August 9th, a B-29 Superfortress named [music] Boxcar lifts off from the island of Tinion. In its belly sits Fat Man, 10,000 lb of bomb, mustard yellow, nearly 5 ft across, signed by 60 personnel before loading. Major Charles Sweeney is at the controls. The mission is to deliver the second atomic bomb [music] to its target. The target is Kokura. The mission is already failing before it clears the runway. A fuel pump [music] malfunction has left roughly 600 gallons of fuel inaccessible in a reserve tank. Fuel they cannot use, [music] weight they must carry. Over the rendevous point, Boxcar circles for 45 minutes, waiting for a photography plane that never arrives. Fuel burning, the margin narrowing over Kokura, smoke. The night before, 224 [music] B29s firebombed the nearby city of Yhata, and the drifting haze is now sitting over the Kokura arsenal. 70% cloud [music] cover. Sweeney makes one ball run, then a second, then a third. Anti-aircraft [music] fire is finding their altitude. Japanese fighter direction radio is coming alive below. The aiming point stays hidden. Boxar turns for [music] Nagasaki. Nagasaki is also covered. Sweeney is looking at overcast [music] sky, a nearly exhausted fuel reserve, and a bomb that cannot be brought home. He is preparing to turn for Okinawa to abort to carry the weapon back when at the last possible moment a gap opens in the clouds. Bombardier Captain Kermit Beaan looks through his sight. I can see my target. At 11:02 in the morning, [music] Fat Man detonates above the Urkami Valley, 1 and a half miles from its intended aiming [music] point. The hills of Nagasaki, the same hills that make the city a natural bowl, an ancient [music] port, the most Christianized city in Japan, contain the blast. The Urakami Cathedral, the largest Catholic [music] cathedral in Asia, is destroyed in the first second. The cloud [music] rises to 60,000 ft. Fat Man is 40% more powerful than the bomb that [music] destroyed Hiroshima. It kills roughly half as many people. The hills save tens of thousands of lives. Geography, not planning, determines who survives. Between 40,000 and 75,000 people die in the [music] first moments. 60,000 more are severely injured. Total deaths by year's end may reach 80,000. Nagasaki was not chosen. It was what remained after everything else went wrong. The return flight nearly kills the crew. Boxgar comes in on three engines. [music] Every emergency flare firing, touching down too fast on a runway too short, bouncing hard, sloowing toward a row of parked aircraft before the pilots wrestle it straight. A second engine dies before the plane stops rolling. No one is there to meet them. No one knew they were coming. In Tokyo at 10:30 that same morning, 32 [music] minutes before Fat Man falls, the Supreme Council convenes. Three events are already converging on the room. Soviet troops crossed into Manuria at midnight. Word of Nagasaki is moving toward the capital, and the emperor in a private [music] meeting the previous afternoon has already made his decision. Prime Minister Canaro Suzuki opens the session. He has just come from the emperor. He tells the council it is impossible to continue [music] the war. Togo urges acceptance of the Potm declaration with one condition, preservation of the emperor's position. Navy Minister Mitsumasa Yonai agrees. They cannot wait for better [music] circumstances. Anomy disagrees. So do Army Chief of Staff General Yoshiro Umeu and Navy Chief of Staff Admiral Simu Toyota. The position is clear. Hiroshima was a one-off. The Americans [music] played their single devastating card. A decisive homeland battle is still possible. Ketsugo still holds. At approximately 1100, a messenger enters the room. Nagasaki. The argument Anami is making that Hiroshima was unique that the Americans had one weapon and have now spent it collapses in the room at that moment. The facts are now beyond disputation. The Americans have more bombs. The invasion strategy assumed the Americans would have to land. If the Americans can simply bomb Japan into rubble from altitude, Ketsugo means nothing. There is no strategy [music] left. And yet, the Hawks do not move. The Big Six remain [music] split 3 to three. The session ends in deadlock. Soviet troops are crossing the Manurion plane. The Americans have more bombs. Six men still cannot agree. Debate continues through the rest of August 9th and into [music] the night. Cabinet session after cabinet session, always the same [music] result. At 2:00 in the morning on August 10th, Prime Minister Suzuki makes a request that has no precedent in the modern history of Japan's constitutional monarchy. He asks the emperor to break the deadlock. The room where this happens is not a grand hall. It is [music] a concrete bunker beneath the Imperial Palace. Low ceiling, lit by bare electric bulbs, the air thick with August heat, and too many men in full dress uniform. The participants sit at long tables. The emperor is seated apart, slightly elevated, facing his council. The only sound is the hum of fans. For his entire reign, with one exception in 1936, when a military coup required [music] his direct intervention, Hirohito has not ruled Japan directly. He has deferred. He has ratified. He has watched the wars catastrophe accumulate for years without acting. He has watched [music] the navy destroyed and the cities burned. The peace faction has known for weeks he favors their position. He has said nothing where [music] it matters. The role of the emperor in Japan's governing theology is [music] not to command but to embody. A living god whose function is consecration, not decision. Every precedent of his reign [music] argues for silence. He does not stay silent. The emperor speaks [music] softly. He has given serious consideration to the situation at home and abroad. He has thought about the soldiers [music] already dead, about what continuing will require of the people who remain, about what Japan will be if the fighting goes on until there is nothing left to protect. He announces his support for Togo's single condition. And then, in a voice multiple accounts will later describe [music] as barely audible, but unmistakable. The time has come when we must bear the unbearable. He weeps during his remarks. The men at the table weep with him. By morning, his decision is official government policy. Japan will offer conditional surrender with the single requirement that the emperor's position be preserved. It is not the end of the crisis. On the morning of August 10th, the Japanese Foreign Ministry transmits its conditional offer of surrender to the Allies. At the same moment, General Anami issues a statement [music] addressed to the army. It calls on every soldier to fight to the last grain of rice. It is printed in newspapers. It reads like a declaration of total war. The army is 3 million armed men who do not yet know their government has offered [music] to surrender. If that truth surfaces before the emperor has spoken publicly, before the [music] offer has been accepted, before there is anything certain to announce, the coup that [music] the peace faction has feared for weeks becomes immediate. Anomy is buying time. He is also [music] still hoping the terms can be improved. The Allied reply, the Burns note [music] does not give him those terms. It says the emperor's authority will be subject to [music] the supreme commander of allied powers. It says the Japanese people will determine their own form of government. For the hawks, this [music] is capitulation dressed in diplomatic language. The debate ignites again. Then the leaflets come. On August 14th, American B-29s released millions of pamphlets [music] over Japan's cities. The leaflets describe the surrender negotiations in plain terms. Negotiations kept entirely secret from the Japanese [music] public and from most of the military. When soldiers in their barracks start reading that their government [music] has been negotiating surrender without the emperor having spoken, without any official announcement, the situation becomes explosive. That night, a group of young army officers seizes the Imperial Palace. [music] They kill its commander. They know Hirohito has recorded his surrender broadcast on photographed cylinders and [music] they move through corridors and store rooms in the dark hunting for those recordings. Destroy them before they air and the piece itself can be destroyed. The recordings are hidden. [music] The officers never find them. By morning, the senior army command refuses to back the mutiny. The coup collapses. At noon on August 15th, [music] 1945, a voice comes out of radios across the Japanese Empire. It is the [music] first time in history that a Japanese emperor has spoken directly to the common people. The voice is thin, precise, formal, delivered in classical Japanese so archaic that [music] many listeners struggle to follow it. The speech refers to the joint [music] declaration. It says the government has accepted its terms. It does not use the word surrender across Japan in the streets, in the fields, on the decks [music] of ships. People do not know at first whether Japan has won or lost. They kneel [music] anyway. Many have never heard his voice before in their lives. He mentions Hiroshima. He mentions [music] Nagasaki. He calls the atomic bomb a new and most cruel bomb. That morning before the broadcast [music] airs, General Ketchika anime dresses in his full military uniform. He sits down on the floor of his home. He commits sepuku. Beside him in his own blood, he leaves a final message. It reads, "Approximately, believing firmly that our sacred land shall never [music] perish, I with my death humbly apologize to the emperor for the great crime." The broadcast [music] goes out at noon. the war. Anami spent six days fighting to continue ends without him. By that afternoon, [music] the army has no figure of sufficient rank and conviction to give resistance a center of gravity. The coup that collapsed in the night has nowhere [music] to reconvene around. On September 2nd, 1945, the formal ceremony takes place [music] aboard the USS Missouri, anchored in Tokyo Bay. The instrument of surrender is signed. [music] The war is officially over. Then the fates. Shiggonori Togo, the man [music] who understood the Potdam declaration before anyone else was willing to accept it, who fought longest [music] and most clearly for an end to the war, was tried by the international military tribunal for the Far East. Convicted of waging wars of aggression, sentenced to [music] 20 years. He died in prison in 1950. General Umezu was tried, convicted, and died in prison in 1949. Prime Minister [music] Suzuki resigned on August the 15th and died in 1948. Admiral Yonai was tried and [music] acquitted. He died that same year. Hirohito renounced his divinity. He signed [music] a new constitution. He visited Hiroshima. He mourned publicly for the rest of his life. He was never tried. He died in [music] 1989. Japan's longest serving monarch, Anami, faced no tribunal. He had already [music] judged himself. The question historians still argue is simple to ask and impossible to answer cleanly. Why did Japan [music] surrender? Was it Hiroshima and Nagasaki? The Soviet invasion? The emperor's unprecedented intervention [music] in a bomb shelter at 2:00 in the morning? The collapse of Ketugo's entire premise? the realization that if the Americans didn't [music] need to land, there was no game left to play. Hirohito himself said on four separate documented occasions [music] that the atomic bomb was the reason. He said it to Togo on August 8th. He said it in his Imperial rescript [music] on August 15th. He said it in a letter to his son in September. He told [music] General Douglas MacArthur that the peace party could not prevail until Hiroshima created a situation which could [music] be dramatized. And yet the historians [music] continue to argue. The emperor's broadcast to the armed forces on August 17th cited Soviet [music] entry as a reason to surrender and did not mention the atomic bombs because Soviet troops were a concrete present threat to commanders on the Asian continent [music] in a way that destroyed cities were not. For those men, the Red Army [music] was not history. It was moving toward them. The answer is probably all of these things combined in proportions that may never be precisely known. Somewhere in a Philippine jungle on August the 15th, [music] 1945, a Japanese soldier named Hiru Onoda was [music] still fighting. His commanding officers had not reached him. The news had not reached him. The orders he carried told him to fight, [music] and so he fought. He kept fighting for 29 years. In 1974, his former commanding officer flew to the Philippines, found him in the jungle where he had spent three [music] decades at war, and personally relieved him of duty. He had been following his orders. The machinery of war, once running, does not know when it's over. The six days between that [music] silence on the radio and the emperor's voice at noon, were an extraordinary human effort to force that machine to stop. It stopped mostly.
